main.title: The Magical Quest Starring Mickey Mouse
main.subtitle: Following Pluto into a strange kingdom
main.summary: The Magical Quest Starring Mickey Mouse is Capcom’s 1992 Super Nintendo platform adventure, recorded in the company’s release history for November of that year.

cards.heading: Following Pluto into a strange kingdom
cards.text: The Magical Quest Starring Mickey Mouse is Capcom’s 1992 Super Nintendo platform adventure, recorded in the company’s release history for November of that year. A search for the missing Pluto draws Mickey into a magical kingdom threatened by Emperor Pete. Running and jumping remain central, but objects and creatures can also become tools: Mickey can grab stunned enemies or useful blocks and throw them. The adventure’s richly colored landscapes combine giant plants, forests and a castle with the visual warmth of a Disney storybook. A simple search for a missing pet grows into a succession of themed challenges.

cards.heading: A wardrobe of new abilities
cards.text: Three special costumes steadily expand Mickey’s abilities. The wizard can charge and release magical shots; the firefighter uses a water jet that can extinguish flames and move certain blocks; the mountaineer uses a rope and grappling hook to climb and swing. Magic and water have supplies that need replenishing, so changing clothes also changes what the player must watch. The original instruction booklet explains these abilities beside photographs of the game, making costume changes a readable part of its design. Music and sound effects are credited jointly to Mari Yamaguchi and Tatsuya Nishimura. The pleasure lies in seeing a familiar character acquire a new way to approach each landscape.

main.title: The Addams Family
main.summary: The Addams Family is a 1992 action-adventure platform game based on the 1991 film of the same name.

cards.heading: A film becomes a platform adventure
cards.text: The Addams Family is a 1992 action-adventure platform game based on the 1991 film of the same name. Developed and published by Ocean Software, it was released for home consoles such as the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, computers such as the Amiga, and handheld consoles such as the Game Boy.

cards.heading: Gomez explores the mansion
cards.text: The player assumes the role of Gomez Addams. His mission is to rescue other members of the Addams family from the clutches of Abigail Craven, who, alongside The Judge and the family attorney Tully Alford, is attempting to seize the Addams' wealth. The game is non-linear, with the player moving throughout the mansion's many inside and outside areas, some of which are hidden. Enemies include bosses each holding a member of the Addams Family hostage, making them necessary to defeat. Power-ups, extra lives, and money are also obtainable.

cards.heading: Ocean and the film adaptation
cards.text: Ocean, a leader in the market of video game adaptations of films in the late 1980s, began development of the tie-in for The Addams Family film in April 1991, before the film switched studios from 20th Century Fox to Paramount Pictures. It was originally planned to be a puzzle game for computer consoles until Paramount requested that Ocean develop a version for the SNES. The final result was that all versions, including the computer versions, were platformers with the same storyline, setting and objective. The game was critically well-received for its graphics, sound, and music, but was widely considered to be a derivative platformer of its time.

main.title: Sonic the Hedgehog 2
main.subtitle: Sonic 2 Turns Speed into Collaboration
main.summary: On November 24, 1992, Sonic the Hedgehog 2 arrives on Genesis in North America and Mega Drive in Europe.

cards.heading: Sonic 2 Turns Speed into Collaboration
cards.text: Sega released the 16-bit Sonic the Hedgehog 2 in Japan on November 21, 1992, followed by North America and Europe on November 24. The sequel introduces Tails and the Spin Dash, expands the levels with parallel routes and adds split-screen competition. Its half-pipe Special Stages offer another style of movement alongside the main platform adventure.

cards.heading: Speed Can Begin from a Standstill
cards.text: The Spin Dash lets Sonic crouch, charge and launch from a standstill. After slowing down or taking a hit, players can rebuild momentum without finding a long run-up. It also changes how ramps and nearby obstacles can be approached. A brief stop becomes preparation for another fast movement.

cards.heading: A Companion Who Follows, Imitates and Makes Mistakes
cards.text: Tails can follow Sonic under computer control or be operated by a second player. He collects rings and attacks enemies, then returns if left behind beyond the camera. The main adventure can continue while a second person joins in without needing to keep perfectly alongside Sonic. His presence gives the journey a partner with a different relationship to the screen.

cards.heading: A Fast Level Needs More Than One Road
cards.text: Broader levels offer routes at different heights, detours and stretches that preserve momentum. Learning the terrain lets players choose a fast trajectory, while slowing down reveals platforms and alternate paths. Chemical Plant combines acceleration with vertical passages, pipes and water sections. The route determines where speed can be maintained and where another kind of timing is needed.

cards.heading: The Track Curves Without Being Truly Three-Dimensional
cards.text: Special Stages send Sonic and Tails along a half-pipe, collecting rings and avoiding obstacles. Scaling and arranging two-dimensional graphics creates the impression of a track extending into depth. Lateral positioning and reaction replace the branching routes of ordinary stages for these short sequences.

cards.heading: The Race Becomes a Direct Comparison
cards.text: Two-player competition splits the screen into compressed views of a course. Both racers can follow their progress directly, with rings, items and overall performance contributing alongside the finish. The reduced image makes a visible compromise in exchange for simultaneous local play.

cards.heading: A Coordinated Release Becomes Part of the Spectacle
cards.text: The North American and European release on November 24 coordinated the Western launch around a single day. Japan had received the 16-bit game three days earlier, while the 8-bit versions followed their own schedules. Sega used the shared Western date to build anticipation for a sequel whose character had become central to the company's identity.

main.title: Final Fantasy V
main.summary: Final Fantasy V is a 1992 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Super Famicom.

cards.heading: A journey to protect the crystals
cards.text: Final Fantasy V is a 1992 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Super Famicom. It is the fifth main installment of the Final Fantasy series. The game begins as a wanderer named Bartz investigates a fallen meteor. There, he encounters several characters, one of whom reveals the danger facing the four Crystals that control the world's elements. These Crystals act as a seal on Exdeath, an evil sorcerer. Bartz and his party must keep the Crystals from being exploited by Exdeath's influence and prevent his resurgence.

cards.heading: New versions across generations
cards.text: It has been ported with minor differences to Sony's PlayStation and Nintendo's Game Boy Advance. An original video animation produced in 1994 called Final Fantasy: Legend of the Crystals serves as a sequel to the events depicted in the game. It was released for the PlayStation Network on April 6, 2011, in Japan. An enhanced port of the game, with new high-resolution graphics and a touch-based interface, was released for iPhone and iPad on March 28, 2013, for Android on September 25 the same year and for Windows on September 24, 2015. A more enhanced re-release of the game as part of the Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster series, was released on November 10, 2021 for Android, iOS, and Windows, for Nintendo Switch and PlayStation 4 on April 19, 2023, and for Xbox Series X/S on September 26, 2024.

cards.heading: Jobs open up character customization
cards.text: Final Fantasy V has been praised for the freedom of customization that the player has over the characters, achieved through the greatly expanded Job System. Despite being released only in Japan at the time, the Super Famicom version sold more than two million copies. The PlayStation version has earned "Greatest Hits" status, selling more than 350,000 copies.

main.title: The G.G. Shinobi II: The Silent Fury
main.subtitle: The crystals and their guardians
main.summary: The G.G. Shinobi II: The Silent Fury is Sega's ninja platform sequel, released for Game Gear in 1992, with the Japanese edition arriving on 11 December.

cards.heading: The crystals and their guardians
cards.text: The G.G. Shinobi II: The Silent Fury is Sega's ninja platform sequel, released for Game Gear in 1992, with the Japanese edition arriving on 11 December. Joe Musashi and his allies seek five elemental crystals taken by the Techno-Warriors and their Black Ninja. The coloured ninja team returns, with each character supplying a particular combination of weapon, movement and magic. Stages can again be approached in different orders, making the campaign's structure depend on which companion has already been rescued and what that companion allows the player to reach.

cards.heading: A rescue opens another route
cards.text: The opening four stages each contain a captured ally and an elemental crystal, but rescuing the ninja does not always make the crystal immediately accessible. A particular ability may be required, sending the player elsewhere before returning with the appropriate companion. The route through the campaign therefore develops across several visits rather than simply ending each stage once. New weapons and revised abilities change the earlier game's combinations, while hidden health upgrades reward looking beyond the direct path. A return journey can reveal an opportunity that the initial rescue left unresolved.

cards.heading: Returning with the right ninja
cards.text: Gathering the first four crystals opens the enemy's main base and the final confrontation over the fifth. By that point, the available team supplies the abilities required to face the remaining obstacles. A password system supports returning to the portable adventure later, fitting the connected campaign into shorter sessions. Yuzo Koshiro and Motohiro Kawashima composed the music. The sequel strengthens the relationship between rescuing characters and exploring stages: another ninja changes the possibilities in several places, so the team grows into a practical map of routes the player can now complete.

main.title: Street Fighter II Turbo
main.summary: Street Fighter II Turbo: Hyper Fighting, released as Street Fighter II Dash Turbo in Japan, is a 1992 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.

cards.heading: Hyper Fighting increases the pace
cards.text: Street Fighter II Turbo: Hyper Fighting, released as Street Fighter II Dash Turbo in Japan, is a 1992 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the third arcade version of Street Fighter II, part of the Street Fighter franchise, following Street Fighter II: Champion Edition, and was initially released as an enhancement kit for that game. Released less than a year after the previous installment, Hyper Fighting introduced a faster playing speed and new special moves for certain characters, as well as further refinement to the character balance.

cards.heading: The final original CPS upgrade
cards.text: Hyper Fighting is the final arcade game in the Street Fighter II series to use the original CP System hardware. It was distributed as an upgrade kit designed to be installed into Champion Edition printed circuit boards. The next game, Super Street Fighter II, uses the CP System's successor, the CP System II.

main.title: E.V.O.: Search for Eden
main.subtitle: A creature of your own
main.summary: E.V.O.: Search for Eden is an action role-playing game in which the character’s body becomes the main form of equipment. Beginning as a fish, the player travels through a fantastic interpretation of Earth’s prehistoric ages under the guidance of Gaia. The journey moves across five periods, opening different possibilities for the creature’s form. Almanic combines side-scrolling movement and combat with the pleasure of visible transformation, allowing the player to build an increasingly unusual animal while pursuing the promise of Eden.

cards.heading: A creature of your own
cards.text: E.V.O.: Search for Eden is an action role-playing game in which the character’s body becomes the main form of equipment. Beginning as a fish, the player travels through a fantastic interpretation of Earth’s prehistoric ages under the guidance of Gaia. The journey moves across five periods, opening different possibilities for the creature’s form. Almanic combines side-scrolling movement and combat with the pleasure of visible transformation, allowing the player to build an increasingly unusual animal while pursuing the promise of Eden.

cards.heading: Spend experience on a body
cards.text: Defeated creatures leave food that supplies evolution points. Those points can be spent on particular body parts, changing both appearance and abilities. An altered jaw improves one kind of attack; changes to the body can affect movement, jumping or resilience. Progress therefore appears directly on the creature rather than being confined to a numerical increase. The player decides which immediate weakness to address and which new form to try, with the available choices changing as the adventure reaches another stage of its fictional natural history.

cards.heading: Adaptation as a way forward
cards.text: Each period has a map of individual stages populated by different organisms. Biting, ramming or jumping can provide ways to deal with them, while avoiding a creature may preserve health. Food, plants and selected transformations offer recovery, connecting survival with the evolution system. Crystals add guidance, points or temporary bodies that let the player experience another form. E.V.O. takes broad liberties with history, but its design makes a clear invitation: experiment with the body, then discover what that body allows in the surrounding world.

main.title: Pocky & Rocky
main.subtitle: Natsume · Super Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Pocky & Rocky is Natsume's Super Nintendo action game about a shrine maiden and a tanuki fighting through a world of monsters inspired by Japanese folklore. Pocky throws paper talismans, while Rocky attacks with leaves. One or two players guide the pair through stages viewed from above, approaching enemies from different directions rather than following a fixed firing lane. Their expressive animation and unusual opponents give the journey a playful character, even when the screen becomes crowded and staying alive demands a carefully chosen movement.

cards.heading: A shrine maiden and an unexpected ally
cards.text: Pocky & Rocky is Natsume's Super Nintendo action game about a shrine maiden and a tanuki fighting through a world of monsters inspired by Japanese folklore. Pocky throws paper talismans, while Rocky attacks with leaves. One or two players guide the pair through stages viewed from above, approaching enemies from different directions rather than following a fixed firing lane. Their expressive animation and unusual opponents give the journey a playful character, even when the screen becomes crowded and staying alive demands a carefully chosen movement.

cards.heading: Keep space for the next attack
cards.text: Both characters combine ranged attacks with a close defensive action, making distance part of the decision at every encounter. A target can be attacked from safety, but an incoming projectile may call for an immediate response nearby. Sliding provides another movement option when the surrounding threats become difficult to avoid. Two players can divide their attention between different enemies, though sharing the same space also requires awareness of the other person's position. Cooperation works best when the partners create room for each other to move.

cards.heading: Folklore with an arcade rhythm
cards.text: The game continues the world introduced by Taito's Kiki Kaikai, reworking it through Natsume's characters and cooperative console action. Temples, shrines and eccentric bosses make the setting recognisable without interrupting the next shooting challenge. Hiroyuki Iwatsuki composed the score. Released in Japan in 1992 and overseas in 1993, it established the Pocky & Rocky name used for the home-console adventures. The memorable partnership gives the familiar work of moving, shooting and avoiding danger a personality that belongs to the two figures sharing the screen.

date_context_only.note: DOOM’s 1993 release anchors a milestone in player-made modifications, not the invention of modding. Earlier examples and later developments are explicitly dated in the article.

main.title: Modding: players become creators
main.subtitle: DOOM and the worlds beyond the original game
main.summary: DOOM’s arrival in 1993 became a landmark for player-made modifications. It did not invent the practice: earlier players had already changed existing games. Its WAD files helped turn that impulse into a lasting culture of new levels, altered artwork and shared experiments.

cards.heading: Before the WAD
cards.text: In 1983, Andrew Johnson and Preston Nevins transformed Castle Wolfenstein into Castle Smurfenstein. Guards became Smurfs, with changes to voices, graphics and setting. Such experiments preceded DOOM's 1993 release, when id Software deliberately separated data in a way that helped a larger community build beyond the original game.

cards.heading: A game that could keep changing
cards.text: DOOM kept level data and other resources in WAD archives, separate from its engine. Community authors could create maps and replace artwork or sounds without rebuilding the entire program. Editors made these structures visible and new levels gave familiar movement and weapons unfamiliar spaces to explore. The later SLADE editor illustrates that continuing craft. This was distinct from another milestone: John Carmack’s release of DOOM engine source code in December 1997.

cards.heading: From modifications to new games
cards.text: Quake carried this culture into another id Software engine, while Half-Life became the foundation for Counter-Strike. Released as a Half-Life mod in 1999, Counter-Strike developed through public betas into a retail release in 2000. A modification could become a game with its own identity and community. Modding opened a route from playing to making: changing a map, testing an idea and sharing the result could matter as much as reaching the ending.

main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 1993
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 1993/1994 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.
